{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
{{infobox person/Wikidata | fetchwikidata=ALL|list=hlist}}
'''Francis James Macdonald Farley''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Past Fellows|url=https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Persons&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28%28text%29%3D%27farley,%20Francis%20James%20Macdonald%27%29|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190426103925/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Persons&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28%28text%29%3D%27farley,%20Francis%20James%20Macdonald%27%29|accessdate=26 April 2019|archive-date = 2019-04-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Crease |first=Robert P. |date=2024 |title=Francis James Macdonald Farley. 13 October 1920—16 July 2018 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.2023.0037 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=77|pages=185–199 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2023.0037 |doi-access=free }}</ref> (13 October 1920 –16 July 2018) was a British physicist. He was elected [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] on 16 March 1972 earning the designation FRS. He was also a Fellow of the Institute of Physics and an honorary fellow of Trinity College Dublin.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/francis-farley-11421/ |title=FrancisFarley &#124; Royal Society |access-date=16 November 2018 |archive-date=9 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181109234555/https://royalsociety.org/people/francis-farley-11421/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was educated at [[Clifton College]] and at [[Clare College, Cambridge]].<ref name="FarleyVij1991">{{cite journal|last1=Farley|first1=F.J.M.|last2=Vij|first2=J.K.|last3=Kocot|first3=A.|last4=Murthy|first4=U.M.S.|last5=Burgess|first5=M.|title=Mechanical load cell based on cavity-controlled microwave oscillators|journal=IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques|volume=39|issue=9|year=1991|pages=1611–1616|issn=0018-9480|doi=10.1109/22.83837|bibcode=1991ITMTT..39.1611F}}</ref> Farley obtained his PhD from [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] in 1950.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Farley |first=Francis James Macdonald |date=1950 |title=Some experiments with an expansion chamber |publisher=University of Cambridge|url=http://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/permalink/f/t9gok8/44CAM_ALMA21431153770003606}}</ref>

During [[World War II]], he designed and made the first X-band microwave radar with 100 ns pulse and a one degree beam which directed the 15" guns at Dover.<ref>[[List of radars|CA No.1 Mk3]] Transmitter & receiver based on NT271, with displays from CA No 1 Mk1.</ref>  It showed shells splashing around the target.  He invented clutter reference [[Doppler radar]] which could see vehicles on land and was used in Italy.<ref>[[List of radars|FA No.1 Mk1]] - Control of artillery fire against ground targets</ref>  As a senior lecturer in Auckland University he was a NZ delegate to the 1955 [[Geneva Summit (1955)|UN conference in Geneva]] on "Peaceful Uses of Atomic Energy".<ref>{{cite conference |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1637031 |title=International Conference on the Peaceful Uses of Atomic Energy |date=1956–1958 |publisher=UN |book-title=Proceedings }}</ref> During a year at Harwell in 1955, he measured the neutron yield from plutonium fission as a function of the incident neutron epithermal energy.{{cn|date=October 2026}}

From 1957 at [[CERN]], he devised and measured the [[muon g-2]] value, the [[anomalous magnetic dipole moment|anomalous magnetic moment]] of the [[muon]], in three successive experiments, inventing the [[muon]] [[storage ring]],<ref>{{cite journal|title=Muon's (g-2): the obstinate deviation from the Standard Model|journal=CERN Bulletin|date=5 December 2011|issue=49–50|url=https://cds.cern.ch/journal/CERNBulletin/2011/50/News%20Articles/1403063}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=What invention is all about|url=http://public-archive.web.cern.ch/public-archive/en/People/Farley-en.html|publisher=CERN}}</ref> as well as performing other accurate tests of special relativity at [[CERN]] (muon lifetime) and more. Known to his reading audience on many of his publications as Farley, he participated in a leading role as one of the only experimental physicists from the CERN experiments in residence full-time at and with the follow-up fourth measurement of [[muon g-2]] at Brookhaven National Laboratory<ref name="Farley2004">{{cite journal|last1=Farley|first1=F|title=The 47 years of muon g−2|journal=Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics|volume=52|issue=1|year=2004|pages=1–83|issn=0146-6410|doi=10.1016/j.ppnp.2003.09.004|bibcode=2004PrPNP..52....1F}}</ref> (the other being [[Frank Krienen]] who joined CERN with Amsterdam Prof & third [[List of Directors General of CERN|Director General]] [[Cornelis Bakker|C J Bakker]] in 1954); Farley continued to provide equally leading guidance for the follow-up fifth [[muon g-2]] measurement at [[Fermilab]] (FNAL) which began data taking around the time of his death.

The physics legacy of Farley by his [[muon g-2]] experiment conducted by hundreds of physicists, engineers, and national laboratory staff, established the [[muon]] as a [[Fermion|spin-1/2]] particle, satisfying the [[Dirac equation]], [[quantum electrodynamics]] (CERN I & II), [[hadron physics]] (CERN III), [[electroweak]], and [[Higgs mechanism|Higgs physics]] (BNL IV), in each of their respective eras. All of these experimental determinations were monumental for the progress of [[particle physics]] theory, enabling the most recent and actively current [[muon g-2|FNAL V experiment]] to significantly constrain the introduction of new particles by theory advances, such as [[supersymmetry]] and [[Dark Matter|dark matter]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/07/science/particle-physics-muon-fermilab-brookhaven.html |title=A Tiny Particle's Wobble Could Upend the Known Laws of Physics |newspaper=The New York Times |date= 7 April 2021|access-date=12 April 2021|last1= Overbye|first1= Dennis}}</ref>

He started working on wave energy in 1976 and filed 14 patents in this area.<ref name=patents/> He was the co-inventor of the Anaconda wave energy device.<ref>{{cite web|title=Peaks and troughs of wave energy: the dreams and the reality – speaker biographies|url=http://royalsociety.org/events/wave-energy-biographies/|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|accessdate=24 October 2011}}</ref>

He won the 1980 [[Hughes Medal]] of the [[Royal Society]] "for his ultra-precise measurements of the muon magnetic moment, a severe test of quantum electrodynamics and of the nature of the muon".<ref>{{cite web|title=Hughes archive winners 1989 – 1902|url=http://royalsociety.org/Content.aspx?id=3286|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|accessdate=5 December 2010}}</ref>

1967–82 he was the academic head of the [[Royal Military College of Science]], Shrivenham. He has been a visiting professor at [[Yale University|Yale]], [[University of Reading]], [[University of New South Wales]] and at [[University of Southampton|Southampton]].{{cn|date=October 2026}}

Moving to France in 1986 he helped the cancer hospital Centre Antoine Lacassagne in [[Nice]] to install a 65 MeV cyclotron for proton therapy.<ref>{{cite conference
| url = http://accelconf.web.cern.ch/AccelConf/c92/papers/vi-05.pdf
| title = Recent activities of the cyclotron laboratory in Nice
| vauthors = Mandrillon P, Brassart, N, Chauvel P, Courdi A, Farley F, Fietier N, Herault J, Tang JY
| date = 1992
| publisher = JACoW
| book-title = Cyclotrons 1992
| pages = 248–251
| location = Vancouver, BC, Canada
| access-date = 26 April 2019
| archive-date = 25 November 2017
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171125063115/http://accelconf.web.cern.ch/AccelConf/c92/papers/vi-05.pdf
| url-status = dead
}}</ref> He designed the beam transport which brings the beam to the patient.  Operating unmodified for 23 years the system has treated over 3000 patients for ocular melanoma with a cure rate of 95%.{{cn|date=October 2026}}

==Publications==
His publications include the Methuen monograph "Elements of Pulse Circuits" (1955)<ref>
{{cite book
 |last=Farley
 |first=Francis
 |date=1955
 |title=Elements of pulse circuits
 |publisher=Methuen
 |place=London
 |pages=151|id={{ASIN|0416406106|country=uk}}
 }}
</ref> translated into French and Spanish and papers on particle physics, relativity, wave energy and cosmology.

[[File:Farley 2013.jpg|thumb|Francis Farley presenting his novel "Catalysed Fusion" in the CERN Library.]]
In 2012, he wrote a romantic novel, Catalysed Fusion, which illustrates life around the accelerators at [[CERN]] and in Geneva<ref>
{{cite book
 |last=Farley
 |first=Francis
 |date=2012
 |title=Catalysed Fusion
 |publisher=CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform 
 |pages=282
 |isbn=978-1481018494}}</ref>

Farley signed more than 50 peer reviewed articles. His nuclear and particle physics related publications are indexed in [[INSPIRE-HEP]]<ref>{{cite web | title = INSPIRE-HEP: Farley, Francis James Macdonald | publisher = [[Stanford Physics Information Retrieval System|INSPIRE-HEP]] | url = https://inspirehep.net/author/profile/F.J.M.Farley.1/ |accessdate = 13 Nov 2019}}</ref>

The [[European Patent Office]] has registered 17 patents with Francis Farley as the inventor.<ref name=patents>{{cite web | publisher =EPO | title =Espacenet: Inventor Francis Farley | url =https://worldwide.espacenet.com/beta/search/family/026293008/publication/GB2212273A?f=publications.pd%3Ain%3D19720101-20171231&q=in%20%3D%20%22FARLEY%20francis%20%20%22 | accessdate =13 Nov 2019 | archive-date =13 November 2019 | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20191113100130/https://worldwide.espacenet.com/beta/search/family/026293008/publication/GB2212273A?f=publications.pd:in%3D19720101-20171231&q=in%20%3D%20%22FARLEY%20francis%20%20%22 | url-status =dead }}</ref>
